strengths: The core algorithmic contribution is genuinely novel and well-motivated: solving continuous-time PL ODEs semi-analytically by computing switching times with interval root finding (branch-and-prune with interval Newton), rather than generic numerical integration. This is a principled exploitation of the PL structure.
The treatment of differentiating through switching times via the implicit function theorem (Eqs. 9-12) is a clean and non-obvious technical solution to training an event-driven solver end-to-end.

The semi-analytical state space analysis (fixed points via Eq. 13, limit cycles via Eq. 14, and the appendix material on saltation operators/Floquet theory) is a differentiating capability relative to both Neural ODEs and discrete-time PLRNNs, and is demonstrated on trained models (Figs. 1-2).

The key practical motivation - handling irregularly sampled data - is convincingly demonstrated (Table 3): the discrete-time PLRNN with linear interpolation breaks down (D_stsp 4.3 vs. 0.26 for cPLRNN) while cPLRNN matches or beats Neural ODEs.
Training speed advantage over Neural ODEs is substantial (Table 2: cPLRNN 21-36s vs. Tsit5 156-175s for comparable performance), addressing a well-known Neural ODE bottleneck.

Evaluation spans a chaotic benchmark (Lorenz-63), a discontinuous system (LIF), and real electrophysiological data, with standard DSR metrics (D_stsp, D_H, MAE), 10 runs per condition, and statistical tests. Hyperparameters, solvers, and metrics are documented in detail, including numerical edge cases (bracketing, overflow, boundary perturbation δt).
The limitations section is honest and specific (numerical instability from ill-conditioned eigendecompositions, root-finding restart costs, the open question of choosing δt).
weaknesses: The central performance claim is only partially supported: on the main chaotic benchmark (Lorenz-63), cPLRNN is significantly worse than the discrete-time PLRNN (p < 0.043) and only on par with the best Neural ODE (no significant difference). The advantage is thus mainly about continuity, speed, and irregular sampling rather than reconstruction quality.

The irregular-sampling advantage is demonstrated on only one synthetic benchmark (LIF). The PLRNN baseline there uses naive linear interpolation - a weak comparison; stronger continuous-time or interpolation-aware baselines (e.g., Latent Neural ODEs designed for irregular sampling, or regularized approaches like Li et al. 2022) are discussed in related work but not compared.

Scalability is a concern: the diagonalizability assumption plus perturbation for non-diagonalizable W, the ill-conditioned eigendecomposition issues, and root-finding restarts at every switching event suggest the method may struggle with larger P or highly stiff systems. Experiments go only up to P=10 ReLUs, and no scaling study is provided.

Only ReLU-based Neural ODEs are compared. The claim that Neural ODEs 'lack tractability' and underperform is cited from prior work, but the benchmark set here is too small to firmly establish that cPLRNN is the best continuous-time DSR option.

There is a conceptual tension in the discontinuity claims: cPLRNN is a continuous vector-field system, while the LIF model is an impact-type system with hard resets; the paper fits it with ReLU approximations rather than the Filippov/impact machinery it itself reviews (Appx. H). This is not deeply analyzed.

Presentation issues reduce polish: duplicated/broken equation numbering in the appendix (Eq. 58/59 appearing before 34-36, an empty Eq. 23), Table 3 header says 'MSE' while the text and other tables use MAE, and Figure 2 uses 'A)' twice for different panels.

No explicit code release is stated, which limits reproducibility for a method paper whose contribution is algorithmic (custom interval-arithmetic root finder, custom implicit-function-theorem gradients in Julia/Zygote).
Statistical margins in the headline comparisons are thin (e.g., p < 0.043 for PLRNN vs. cPLRNN), and the practical significance of these differences is not discussed.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: exploiting the piecewise-linear structure of ReLU-based RNNs to obtain closed-form solutions within each linear region, replacing numerical ODE integration with exact region solutions plus interval-arithmetic root finding for switching times. This is a clean and, to my knowledge, novel algorithmic contribution for continuous-time DSR.

The differentiation-through-root-times derivation via the implicit function theorem (Eqs. 9-12) is technically sound and a non-trivial implementation detail that is often glossed over in similar work.

The semi-analytical computation of topological invariants (fixed points via SCYFI adaptation, limit cycles via the multi-region boundary-value formulation in Eq. 14) is a meaningful step toward interpretable, analyzable learned dynamical models, and the Lorenz fixed-point recovery from chaotic trajectories alone (Fig. 1) is a nice demonstration of topological generalization.

Experiments include 10 training runs per configuration with median/MAD reporting and Mann-Whitney U tests, and hyperparameters/training details are documented in Appendix D-F, which supports reproducibility.
The limitations section is honest about numerical fragility (ill-conditioned eigendecompositions), the fixed perturbation δt, and root-finding restart costs.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the claims. Only three benchmarks (Lorenz-63, simulated LIF, one cortical neuron recording) with latent dimensions M=20-25 and at most P=10 ReLUs. Scalability to higher-dimensional systems or many switching regions (where the sequential root-finding and 2^P region growth become bottlenecks, as acknowledged) is not demonstrated.

Missing key baselines for the central selling point. The paper motivates cPLRNNs primarily by irregularly sampled data, yet the irregular-sampling experiment is run only on the synthetic LIF system, and the cited methods designed exactly for this setting (Latent Neural ODEs, Neural CDEs, SDE-based approaches; Rubanova et al., Kidger et al.) are discussed in Related Work but never compared. The discrete PLRNN baseline on irregular data is a weak strawman (linear interpolation into fixed bins) rather than a fair attempt to adapt it.

The claimed advantage over discrete-time PLRNNs on regularly sampled data does not materialize: in Table 1 the standard PLRNN dominates cPLRNN on every metric, and the paper must fall back on training speed relative to Neural ODEs. The headline contribution thus rests mainly on one synthetic irregular-sampling experiment whose data is generated by simply deleting 90% of points from a regular grid, with a differently tuned teacher-forcing interval (τ=3 vs 25), raising fairness questions.

Robustness and approximation caveats undermine the 'exact/precise solver' narrative: diagonalizability is assumed and non-diagonalizable W_Ωk matrices are 'slightly perturbed' (which alters the vector field), gradients are discarded for tangential roots, a hand-fixed δt=0.0001 is used to force boundary crossings, and divergences occur in practice. No error analysis or quantification of how often these fallbacks trigger is provided.

Statistical reporting has issues: differences with p > 0.048 are declared non-significant without multiple-comparison correction, and the irregular-sampling LIF results conflate the model class advantage with the specific binning choice for the baseline.

Presentation is sloppy in places, which erodes confidence: Section E appears twice (Numerical Solvers and Benchmark Systems), appendix equation numbering is out of order ((58) before (34)), Figure 2's caption labels both panels 'A)', Table 1's header says 'latent dimensions P' when P denotes PL units, and the LIF reset discontinuity (an impact system by the paper's own classification in H.1) is glossed over when claiming cPLRNN handles 'systems with discontinuities'.
No code release is stated despite the method's dependence on a bespoke interval-Newton root finder and custom Zygote gradients, which are difficult to reproduce from the description alone.

strengths: The core contribution—a continuous-time PLRNN trained via semi-analytical switching-time computation rather than numerical integration—is technically sound and well-motivated. Exploiting the PL structure to obtain closed-form solutions per linear region, locating switching times with a rigorous interval-Newton branch-and-prune root finder (Appx. C), and differentiating through implicit switching times via the implicit function theorem (Eqs. 9–12) is a clever and carefully executed algorithmic design.

The semi-analytical analysis pipeline for trained models is a genuine value-add: adaptation of SCYFI to continuous-time fixed points, and the limit-cycle formulation as a well-posed root-solving problem over region sequences (Eq. 14) with trust-region/variable-projection solvers, provides interpretability that generic Neural ODEs lack. Demonstrating inferred fixed points and limit cycles on Lorenz-63, LIF, and real electrophysiology (Fig. 2) is convincing as a 'topological out-of-domain' capability.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably rigorous for its scope: standard DSR metrics (Dstsp, DH, MAE), 10 training runs per configuration, median ± MAD reporting, Mann-Whitney U tests, three Neural ODE solvers as baselines, and a real-world dataset with delay embedding. The irregular-sampling experiment (Table 3) clearly demonstrates the motivating use case, where the discrete-time PLRNN with interpolation breaks down (Dstsp 4.3 vs 0.26).

The paper is honest about limitations: admitted numerical instabilities from ill-conditioned eigendecompositions, the heuristic fixed δt perturbation (Appx. C.4), restart costs of root finding, and explicitly notes that cPLRNN is slightly worse than the discrete PLRNN on regular grids. The appendix is thorough (interval arithmetic details, all hyperparameters), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Benchmark breadth is limited. The empirical claims rest on two low-dimensional simulated systems (Lorenz-63 with M=20; 1-d LIF) and a single real-world dataset. Scalability to higher-dimensional attractors, higher P (exponentially many regions, repeated eigendecompositions and root-finding restarts), longer sequences, or noisier observations is not demonstrated and is plausible to be problematic given the acknowledged numerical fragility.

The irregular-sampling comparison against the discrete PLRNN is arguably a weak baseline: binning/linear interpolation is the most naive treatment, and established irregularly-sampled baselines (Latent ODE, Neural CDE, GRU-D, rSLDS variants) are not included. The 'clear practical advantage' for irregular data is thus established only relative to a straw-man adaptation and Neural ODEs.

On regularly sampled data—the regime where most DSR work operates—the cPLRNN does not beat the standard discrete-time PLRNN (statistically worse on Lorenz-63, p < 0.043; comparable on LIF and neuron data), and its advantage over Tsit5 Neural ODEs is largely in training speed (Table 2), measured only in a sequential Julia implementation. Whether the speedup holds under batched/parallel training or against more recent fast Neural ODE training schemes (e.g., with Jacobian/kinetic regularization) is unverified.

Several modeling assumptions are handled by heuristics that could affect reliability: the diagonalizability assumption with ad hoc perturbation of non-diagonalizable WΩk, fixed δt = 0.0001 that could 'jump across further boundaries and thereby alter the dynamics' (the authors' own words), and gradient discarding at tangential roots. No systematic ablation or analysis of how often these edge cases occur or how they bias inference is provided.

The real-data result (Table 4) shows only marginal differences among models (e.g., DH 0.474 vs 0.466 for PLRNN), so the practical benefit on empirical data is not compellingly established, and no quantified evaluation of the inferred limit cycle against ground-truth spiking statistics is given beyond visual inspection.

Code availability is not explicitly stated in the manuscript; given the substantial custom numerics (interval root finding, Zygote custom derivatives), reproducibility without released code would be difficult despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The core contribution is genuinely novel: a continuous-time formulation of PLRNNs (cPLRNN) with a semi-analytical solver that exploits the PL structure, replacing numerical integration with interval-arithmetic root finding for switching times, and implicit-function-theorem differentiation through switching events. This is a well-motivated and technically substantive algorithmic contribution.

The paper goes beyond training/simulation to provide analysis tools grounded in the PL continuous-time DS literature (Coombes et al., 2024): semi-analytical equilibrium detection (adapting SCYFI) and exact limit-cycle localization via the region-sequence/multiple-shooting formulation (Eq. 14). Demonstrating inferred bistability on real cortical neuron data is a nice illustration of the scientific-utility claim.

Evaluation is comparatively broad for the DSR setting: chaotic Lorenz-63, a discontinuous LIF model, real electrophysiology, and irregularly sampled PhysioNet heartbeats; baselines include Neural ODEs with three solvers, Latent ODE, Neural CDE, SINDy, and the discrete-time PLRNN; standard DSR metrics (Dstsp, DH, prediction time, MAE) with significance tests.

The central practical claims are supported by evidence: cPLRNN matches the best Neural ODE (Tsit5) on Lorenz-63 while training several times faster (Table 2), and clearly outperforms the discrete-time PLRNN under irregular sampling (Tables 3, 7), which is the natural use case for a continuous-time model.

Appendices provide substantial algorithmic detail (interval Newton method, branch-and-prune root finding, scaling analyses in Figs. 8-9, robustness analysis of limit-cycle detection in Fig. 7), and code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.

The limitations section is candid and informative: numerical fragility from ill-conditioned eigen-decompositions, the fixed perturbation δt heuristic, restarted root-finding costs, possible missed invariant sets, and restriction to shallow RNNs.
weaknesses: On regularly sampled data, the headline performance is parity, not superiority: cPLRNN is statistically slightly worse than the discrete-time PLRNN on Lorenz-63 and comparable to Neural ODE (Tsit5). The decisive advantage is confined to the irregular-sampling regime, where key baselines are declared 'essentially not able to deal with this problem setup' rather than carefully adapted, weakening the strength of those comparisons.

The irregular-sampling empirical evidence is somewhat narrow: the LIF irregular experiment uses only 10% subsampled points of a simple 1D linear-with-reset system, and the PhysioNet comparison to Neural ODE methods is restricted to a single subject with the most data points (Table 8). A stronger demonstration on richer irregularly-sampled real data would be needed to substantiate the broader forecasting claim in Section 4.5.

Training robustness concerns are real, not just cosmetic: the method relies on diagonalizability assumptions, random perturbation of non-diagonalizable region matrices with discarded gradients (Algo. 3), a hand-tuned boundary-crossing perturbation δt = 0.0001, and occasional numerical instability terminating optimization. Although Fig. 9 shows ill-conditioning is rare, the paper does not quantify the failure rate of full training runs across seeds for the cPLRNN (diverging runs are excluded for baselines but not reported for cPLRNN).

Reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in some comparisons: for Latent ODE and Neural CDE only 'the best value across all training runs' is provided (vs. median ± MAD for others), diverging-run exclusions differ across models and bias results in different directions, and the noise injection used to make Dstsp applicable to limit cycles introduces an additional modeling choice that is not ablated.

Presentation issues: the supplementary equation numbering jumps (Eq. 36 to Eq. 58), Table 9 labels latent dimension as 'P' (vs. 'number of PL units P' elsewhere), and the conclusion overstates the generality of results ('strong contender for irregular time series forecasting') relative to the limited evidence.

Scalability to larger, deeper models is addressed only indirectly: runtimes scale linearly with M and sublinearly with P (Fig. 8), but all benchmarks use small M (20-30) and small P (2-10); the claimed irrelevance of scaling with P leans on citations from the same group rather than new evidence.

The paper is primarily of interest to the DSR/PL dynamical systems community; the contribution is specialized, and the incremental nature of the empirical gains (on regular data) means its impact outside this niche may be modest.

strengths: Genuine technical contribution: the paper derives an analytic solution for the linear ODE within each PL subregion and reduces the continuous-time integration problem to root-finding for switching times, with gradients through switching times handled via the implicit function theorem (Eqs. 10-12). This is a clean, well-motivated idea that removes a real bottleneck of Neural ODE training.

The state-space analysis machinery (semi-analytic fixed points via Eq. 13 and exact limit-cycle locations via the multi-region constraint system Eq. 14) is a distinctive capability that neither discrete PLRNNs nor generic Neural ODEs offer as directly, and the robustness analysis in Fig. 7 and runtime figures support its practicality.

Comprehensive experimental design for the core claims: Lorenz-63, a discontinuous LIF system, a real electrophysiological recording, and irregularly sampled PhysioNet data, with appropriate DSR metrics (Dstsp, DH, prediction time) and multiple ODE solvers as baselines.

The irregular-sampling advantage is real and clearly demonstrated: on the irregularly sampled LIF data (Table 3) the standard PLRNN breaks down (Dstsp 15.3 vs 6.6) while cPLRNN is essentially unaffected, which directly supports the paper's central motivation.

Honest and thorough limitations section (numerical fragility of eigen-decompositions, restart costs after switching events, possible missed invariant sets, restriction to shallow RNNs), plus reported diverging runs and statistical tests in the main tables; code availability is stated.
Training speed (Table 2) and scaling analyses (Figs. 8-9) are concrete and support the efficiency claim relative to Neural ODEs.
weaknesses: The headline performance claim is weaker than the framing suggests: on regular sampling the cPLRNN is not better than its discrete-time predecessor (e.g., Lorenz-63 Table 1: Dstsp 0.37 vs 0.24; DH 0.116 vs 0.079; both differences significant), and on the chaotic benchmark it is statistically indistinguishable from the best Neural ODE (Tsit5). The paper's main empirical win is confined to the irregular-sampling setting.

Novelty relative to existing event-detection/hybrid ODE tooling is not adequately delineated. Root-finding at switching surfaces is closely related to event handling in standard ODE integrators (e.g., DifferentialEquations.jl continuous callback/event detection), and the continuous PLRNN itself (Eq. 5) is essentially the classical ReLU-based recurrent formulation used in neural population models. The paper should position its contribution more carefully against these established techniques.

Some 'numerical integration is bypassed' rhetoric is overstated: the method replaces one numerical procedure (ODE stepping) with another (interval-Newton root finding plus eigen-decompositions per subregion), and the limitations section concedes fragility (ill-conditioned eigen-decompositions, heuristic perturbation delta_t = 1e-4, gradient discarding for non-diagonalizable matrices, a 1e-10 duplicate-eigenvalue threshold). These workarounds undermine the claim of a 'much more precise' procedure.

Real-data evidence is thin relative to the motivation: the PhysioNet comparison against Neural ODEs is on a single subject (Table 8) with only five runs, and the cortical-neuron experiment relies on delay embedding with somewhat qualitative fixed-point/limit-cycle interpretation (Fig. 2B). Broader and more systematic real-world evaluation of the irregular-sampling claim would substantially strengthen the paper.

Several baselines are weak/strawman for the central question: Latent ODE and Neural CDE are known not to support autonomous long-term roll-outs, so their inclusion pads the tables without informing the core comparison; conversely, modern alternatives for irregular series or continuous-time DS learning (e.g., neural SDEs, trained-decoder SSMs) are cited but not compared.

The limit-cycle detection procedure requires the correct sequence of visited subregions R and initial guesses as input (Sect. 3.2); the paper does not fully specify how these are obtained in practice for trained models, which limits reproducibility of that contribution.

The method currently supports only shallow ReLU-based architectures with an identity/linear decoder in all reported experiments; generalization of the training algorithm to more expressive observation models is asserted but not demonstrated.

Presentation issues: the mixture of forward references to tools from Coombes et al. (2024) (Appx. H) that are described but not actually applied to trained models dilutes the claimed 'theory harvest'; and dependence on several in-press/unpublished works from the same group (e.g., 2026-dated citations) for key supporting claims (scaling with P, universal approximation) weakens self-containedness.

strengths: The core idea is novel and well-motivated: converting the SOTA class of discrete-time PLRNNs into continuous-time ODE models while exploiting their piecewise-linear structure to obtain semi-analytical solutions, thereby avoiding numerical integration entirely. This directly addresses a genuine gap (handling irregularly sampled data and interpolation to arbitrary time points).

The algorithmic contributions are substantive and carefully engineered: analytic per-region solutions (Eq. 6-7), interval Newton branch-and-prune root finding for the first switching time (Appx. C), and a customized implicit-function-theorem derivative for gradients through switching times (Eq. 9-12) show real technical depth beyond a straightforward Neural ODE re-formulation.

The semi-analytical computation of equilibria (via SCYFI adaptation) and exact limit cycles (Eq. 14, with Trust-Region/Variable Projection solving) is a compelling interpretability feature, demonstrated on simulated and real spiking data (Fig. 2), with an impressive robustness analysis (Fig. 7).

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: chaotic Lorenz-63, a discontinuous LIF system, real electrophysiological recordings, and irregularly sampled PhysioNet heartbeats, with appropriate DSR metrics (Dstsp, DH, prediction time), statistical tests, ablations over P and M, scaling analysis (Fig. 8), and multiple Neural ODE solvers as baselines.

Honest and detailed limitations section (numerical robustness of eigendecompositions, root-finding restarts, initialization sensitivity of the cycle detection, restriction to shallow RNNs), and code availability supports reproducibility. Hyperparameters and solver details are documented at a level that would allow reimplementation.
weaknesses: On the flagship chaotic benchmark (Lorenz-63), the cPLRNN is not better than either baseline: it matches the best Neural ODE (Tsit5) but is statistically worse than the discrete-time PLRNN (p < 0.043, Table 1). The headline speed advantage (Table 2) comes with somewhat lower reconstruction quality on regular data, so the practical case rests mainly on the irregular-sampling regime, which is demonstrated on fewer, partly small-scale setups (e.g., only one PhysioNet subject used for Neural ODE comparisons in Tab. 8).

Numerical fragility is non-trivial: training depends on perturbing non-diagonalizable/ill-conditioned matrices and discarding gradients in those cases (Appx. D.2), a fixed perturbation δt = 0.0001 whose 'best choice is still an open question' (Appx. C.4), and optimization failures the authors themselves admit are not fully resolved. This weakens the claim of a reliable 'much more efficient and precise procedure'.

Comparison fairness is uneven in places: Latent ODE and Neural CDE results are reported as 'best value across all runs' while other models report medians, and diverging runs of baselines are excluded (which the authors note biases results in favor of those baselines, but the heterogeneous reporting makes precise comparison difficult). Some significance statements are marginal (e.g., 'all p < 0.06' in Sect. 4.4).

Much of the analytical machinery (saltation operators, Floquet theory for PL systems, fixed-point/limit-cycle theory) is adapted from Coombes et al. (2024) and prior PLRNN work (SCYFI, Eisenmann et al. 2023); the framing as developing 'theory for continuous-time PLRNNs' somewhat overstates the originality relative to the genuinely new parts (the solver and differentiation scheme).

Presentation issues reduce polish: equation numbering jumps in Appendix G (37 to 58), a naming inconsistency ('cALRNN' in Fig. 8 vs. cPLRNN elsewhere), Table 1 caption ambiguity ('10 × 100 model trainings × trajectories' vs. '10 model trainings' elsewhere), and minor typographical errors. The discrete PLRNN remains ~7x faster to train than the cPLRNN (Table 2), so users without irregular data have little incentive to switch.
